title: Two Pointers
summary: Replace nested O(n²) loops on sorted arrays, strings, or linked lists with two coordinated indices moving in O(n) time and O(1) space.
objectives: Understand the monotonicity prerequisite required for two-pointer pair elimination.
Master opposite-direction converging pointers for sorted pair sum and palindrome checks.
Master same-direction fast and slow pointers for in-place compaction and Floyd's cycle detection.
Implement Dutch National Flag 3-way partitioning in a single pass.
prerequisites: Basic Big-O notation for time and auxiliary space

complexity.time: O(n) amortized time across all variants as each index is traversed at most a constant number of times
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary space, keeping state strictly in two or three pointer variables
complexity.tradeOffs: Requires monotonic input ordering; for unsorted data, sorting first requires O(n log n) time.

commonMistakes: Attempting opposite-direction pair sum on an unsorted array without sorting first.
Using `left <= right` vs `left < right` inconsistently and double-counting the middle element.
Overwriting array values during in-place compaction before reading them.
Failing to skip duplicate values when enumerating unique combinations like 3Sum.
keyTakeaways: Monotonicity is the prerequisite: pair elimination only works when advancing an index predictably eliminates unneeded search space.
Opposite-direction pointers converge to search sorted ranges or verify palindromes in O(n) time.
Same-direction pointers (slow/fast) compact arrays in-place or detect cycles (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm).
Dutch National Flag (3 pointers) partitions an array into three distinct slices in a single pass.
sources: Introduction to Algorithms (CLRS) - Two Pointers and Partitioning
LeetCode Curated Algorithm Patterns - Two Pointers & Fast-Slow
changeSummary: Canonical reference concept manifest for Two Pointers with comprehensive theory and recall questions.

recallQuestions.prompt: Under what conditions can the Two Pointers opposite-ends technique find a pair summing to target in O(n) time and O(1) space?
options: The input array must have no duplicate elements.
The input array must be sorted in monotonic order.
The input array must contain only positive numbers.
The input array must have an even length.
recallQuestions.explanation: Opposite-direction two pointers requires monotonic ordering (e.g. sorted ascending). If sum < target, left advances to increase sum; if sum > target, right retreats. Without monotonicity, pair elimination is invalid.

recallQuestions.prompt: In the Dutch National Flag algorithm (3-way partition), why is the inspection index `mid` NOT incremented when `nums[mid] === 2` is swapped with `nums[high]`?
options: Because `high` is already guaranteed to contain a 0.
Because the element swapped from `high` has not been inspected yet and could be a 0, 1, or 2.
Because `mid` always lags behind `low` by at least one index.
Because incrementing `mid` would violate the sorted invariant of `low`.
recallQuestions.explanation: When swapping `nums[mid]` with `nums[high]`, the value originally at `high` was unexamined. It might be a 0, 1, or 2, so `mid` must examine this newly received element in the next iteration before advancing.

recallQuestions.prompt: In Floyd's Cycle-Finding Algorithm on linked lists, if `fast` moves at 2 steps per iteration and `slow` moves at 1 step, what guarantees they must meet if a cycle exists?
options: The fast pointer reverses direction upon reaching the tail.
Once both are in the cycle of length C, the relative distance between them decreases by exactly 1 in each iteration.
The slow pointer stops at the midpoint of the cycle until fast catches up.
The hash table tracks visited node memory addresses.
recallQuestions.explanation: Inside a cycle of length C, each step reduces the relative distance between `fast` and `slow` by (2 - 1) = 1. Therefore, `fast` is mathematically guaranteed to close the gap and meet `slow` in at most C steps.
